html:
The Housing and Development Board was set up in 1960 to replace Singapore's crowded slums and squatter villages with public flats. Today about four in five Singaporeans live in its estates.

It built tens of thousands of flats within a few years, and in 1964 began selling them to their tenants on long leases, paid from compulsory savings. From 1989 each block was given quotas by race, to stop ethnic enclaves.

Owning a flat gave families a stake in the new state that Lee Kuan Yew built after independence. The new towns, with markets, schools and hawker centres, became the setting of everyday life.
